topics: 📜 What Must Be Said — covenant, Torah, and the house of David; Rav's leniency and Rav Sheshet's anger
👑 Sovereignty in 'Who Is Good and Does Good' — one, two, or three mentions of malkhut
🔚 One Ending per Blessing — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi vs Levi, and how to close 'Who builds Jerusalem'
🕯️ Forgot Shabbat or a Festival — Rav Giddel's replacement blessings and when one must start over
🌙 Rosh Ḥodesh in Grace vs the Amida — Shmuel's distinction between obligation and option
🥚 Olive-bulk or Egg-bulk — Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda seem to switch sides; the new mishna on zimmun formulas

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Getting the Words of Grace Right
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 49a–49b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל שֶׁלֹּא אָמַר בְּרִית וְתוֹרָה בְּבִרְכַּת הָאָרֶץ וּמַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד בְּ״בוֹנֵה יְרוּשָׁלָיִם״ — לֹא יָצָא יְדֵי חוֹבָתוֹ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf is about the precise wording of Grace after Meals. It lists the themes that must appear — covenant and Torah in the blessing of the land, the house of David in 'Who builds Jerusalem' — and shows Rav Ḥisda embarrassed at the Exilarch's table for leaving them out. It debates how many times God's sovereignty must be mentioned in the fourth blessing, whether a blessing may close with two themes, and what to do when Shabbat, a Festival, or Rosh Ḥodesh was forgotten. It ends by reconciling Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on olive-bulk versus egg-bulk, and opens a new mishna on how the zimmun formula grows with the size of the group.

slides.title: 📜 Themes That Must Appear in Grace after Meals
slides.subtitle: Requirements, blunders, and one lenient opinion

boxes.title: Required
items: Pelimu: mention the covenant before the Torah — the Torah was given with three covenants, circumcision with thirteen
Rabbi Abba: thanksgiving at the beginning and end of the blessing; never fewer than one, or it is reprehensible
Baraita, supporting Rabbi Il'a in the name of Rabbeinu: without covenant and Torah in the blessing of the land and the house of David in 'Who builds Jerusalem', one has not fulfilled his obligation

boxes.title: Marks of an ignoramus
items: Concluding the blessing of the land with 'Who bequeaths lands'
Concluding 'Who builds Jerusalem' with 'Who redeems Israel'
Both corrupt the intention of the blessing

boxes.title: Rav's leniency
items: Rav Ḥananel in Rav's name: one who omitted covenant, Torah, and sovereignty has still fulfilled his obligation
Reason: covenant does not apply to women; Torah and sovereignty apply neither to women nor to slaves
Rav Ḥisda relied on this at the Exilarch's house, and Rav Sheshet 'stiffened his neck over me like a snake'
Rabbi Zeira: you abandoned all those tanna'im and amora'im and followed Rav?!

callout.label: Rav Ḥisda's humility:
callout.text: Asked by Rabbi Zeira to teach Mishna, he answered: I have not yet learned Grace after Meals, and I should teach Mishna?

slides.title: 🔚 May a Blessing Conclude with Two Themes?
slides.subtitle: Rabba bar Rav Huna's double ending sparks a review of every double-sounding conclusion

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: At the Exilarch's house Rabba bar Rav Huna opened 'Who builds Jerusalem' with one theme and closed with two — Jerusalem and the redemption of Israel. Great fortitude, to conclude with two! Rabbi taught: one does not conclude with two.

lines.speaker: Levi
lines.text: But we say 'for the land and for the food'!

lines.speaker: Rabbi
lines.text: That is one theme: the land that produces food. Likewise 'for the land and for the fruit' — the land that produces fruit.

lines.speaker: Levi
lines.text: 'Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons'? 'Who sanctifies Israel and the New Moons'?

lines.speaker: Rabbi
lines.text: Israel, who sanctify the seasons; Israel, who sanctify the New Moons.

lines.speaker: Levi
lines.text: 'Who sanctifies Shabbat, Israel, and the seasons'?

lines.speaker: Rabbi
lines.text: Except for that one — there it is all one matter, the sanctity of the day. Jerusalem and redemption are two distinct matters. And the reason: אֵין עוֹשִׂין מִצְוֹת חֲבִילוֹת חֲבִילוֹת, one does not perform mitzvot in bundles.

callout.label: So how do we close the third blessing?
callout.text: Rav Sheshet: match the opening — 'have compassion on Israel' closes with 'Who redeems Israel'; 'have compassion on Jerusalem' closes with 'Who builds Jerusalem'. Rav Naḥman: always 'Who builds Jerusalem', for 'The Lord builds Jerusalem; He gathers in the exiles of Israel' (Ps. 147:2) — building Jerusalem is Israel's redemption. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda permits even 'Who redeems Israel'.

slides.title: 👑 How Many Times Is God's Sovereignty Mentioned?
slides.subtitle: The status of 'Who is good and does good' decides everything

nodes.content: ❓ Abba Yosei ben Dostai and the Rabbis: does 'Who is good and does good' require mention of God's sovereignty?

columns.label: Requires malkhut
columns.content: It is rabbinic, an independent blessing — so it needs its own mention of sovereignty.

columns.label: Does not require
columns.content: It is Torah law, a continuation of the preceding blessings.

nodes.content: 💬 Rabbi Yoḥanan (via Rabba bar bar Ḥana): it requires sovereignty. But Rabbi Yoḥanan already said every blessing without sovereignty is no blessing — what is new?
💡 Rabbi Zeira: it needs two mentions — one for itself and one for 'Who builds Jerusalem', which lacks it.

🔁 Then it should need three, adding one for the blessing of the land! Answer: the land blessing is juxtaposed to a preceding blessing and needs none — and so, in principle, is 'Who builds Jerusalem'. But having mentioned the kingdom of David, it is not proper to omit the kingdom of Heaven.
✅ Rav Pappa's version: 'Who is good and does good' needs two mentions of sovereignty besides its own — for Jerusalem and for the land.

slides.title: 🕯️ Forgot to Mention the Day? Rav Giddel's Fixes
slides.subtitle: Reported before Rav Huna, in Rav's name, with Rabbi Zeira listening behind
rows: 'Blessed… Who gave Shabbatot for rest to His people Israel with love, as a sign and a covenant; Blessed… Who sanctifies the Shabbat'
Rav Naḥman started Grace over; Rabbi Menashya bar Taḥlifa in Rav's name: the short blessing works only before beginning 'Who is good and does good' — after that, return to the beginning
'Blessed… Who gave Festivals to His people Israel for joy and for commemoration; Blessed… Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons'
Same rule: Shabbat and Festivals are days one cannot refrain from eating, so an error sends one back
'Blessed… Who gave New Moons to His people Israel for commemoration' — Rabbi Zeira did not know whether 'joy' was said, whether it closed with a blessing, or whether it was Rav Giddel's own or Rav's
Shmuel: in the Amida one repeats; in Grace after Meals one does not

callout.label: Why the difference for Rosh Ḥodesh?
callout.text: Rav Naḥman reasoned it out for Rav Amram: the Amida is an obligation, so an error requires repetition; Grace depends on eating, and if one wishes he does not eat — so it is not repeated. On Shabbat and Festivals, when one must eat, the error does require starting over.

slides.title: 🥚 Olive-bulk vs Egg-bulk: Did Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda Switch Sides?
slides.subtitle: The end of the chapter and the opening of the next mishna

steps.content: 1️⃣ Our mishna: how much must one eat to obligate a zimmun? An olive-bulk (Rabbi Meir); Rabbi Yehuda says an egg-bulk
2️⃣ Elsewhere: one who left Jerusalem with consecrated meat past Mount Scopus burns it in place; before that he returns — for an egg-bulk (Rabbi Meir) or an olive-bulk (Rabbi Yehuda). The opposite!
3️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan: the opinions are reversed in one of the sources

4️⃣ Abaye: do not reverse. Here they interpret verses — Rabbi Meir: 'you shall eat' is eating (an olive-bulk), 'and be satisfied' is drinking; Rabbi Yehuda: 'eat and be satisfied' is eating that satisfies, an egg-bulk
5️⃣ There they reason logically — Rabbi Meir: returning is like impurity, which needs an egg-bulk; Rabbi Yehuda: returning is like the prohibition, which applies to an olive-bulk

6️⃣ New mishna: with three say 'Let us bless'; with three and himself, 'Bless'; with ten, 'Let us bless our God'; with a hundred, 'the Lord our God'; with a thousand, 'the God of Israel'; with ten thousand, '…the God of Hosts, Who sits upon the cherubs, for the food that we have eaten'

7️⃣ Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: the blessing follows the size of the crowd — 'In assemblies bless God' (Ps. 68:27). Rabbi Akiva: as in the synagogue, many or few say 'Bless the Lord'. Rabbi Yishmael: 'Bless the Lord, the blessed One'

callout.label: Shmuel's principle:
callout.text: לְעוֹלָם אַל יוֹצִיא אָדָם אֶת עַצְמוֹ מִן הַכְּלָל — one should never exclude himself from the collective. The Gemara asks: but the mishna says 'with three and himself, he says Bless'! The answer begins: say that the mishna means…

summary.principle: Grace after Meals must carry its required themes — covenant, Torah, the house of David, God's sovereignty — each blessing with a single ending, and a forgotten Shabbat or Festival sends one back to the beginning once 'Who is good and does good' has begun.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Covenant and Torah in the blessing of the land, the house of David in 'Who builds Jerusalem' — omit them and you have not fulfilled your obligation (Rav alone is lenient)
🔚 Rabbi: no blessing concludes with two themes — mitzvot are not bundled; Rav Naḥman: close with 'Who builds Jerusalem' (Ps. 147:2)
👑 'Who is good and does good' carries extra mentions of sovereignty for the blessings before it

columns.content: 🕯️ Forgot Shabbat/Festival: say 'Blessed… Who gave…' — unless 'Who is good' was begun, then start over
🌙 Forgot Rosh Ḥodesh: repeat the Amida, not Grace — eating is optional

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Abaye keeps Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda consistent — verses decide the zimmun measure, logic decides the return of consecrated meat

quiz.q: Why did Rav Sheshet become angry with Rav Ḥisda at the Exilarch's house?
o: Rav Ḥisda concluded a blessing with two themes
Rav Ḥisda omitted covenant, Torah, and sovereignty from Grace after Meals
Rav Ḥisda forgot to mention Shabbat
Rav Ḥisda recited Grace without having eaten grain
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda relied on Rav's view that omitting covenant, Torah, and sovereignty still fulfills the obligation. Rabbi Zeira told him Rav Sheshet was right to be angry, since he had abandoned many tanna'im and amora'im to follow Rav.

quiz.q: What reason does the Gemara give for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's rule that one does not conclude a blessing with two themes?
o: A long conclusion distracts those answering amen
One does not perform mitzvot in bundles
The Torah only mentions one theme per blessing
Two themes would require two mentions of God's sovereignty
quiz.e: The Gemara explains: 'ein osin mitzvot ḥavilot ḥavilot' — mitzvot are not bundled together; each blessing has its own single ending.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman, how does one conclude the third blessing of Grace even if he opened with 'Have compassion on Israel'?
o: 'Who redeems Israel'
'Who bequeaths lands'
'Who builds Jerusalem', because 'The Lord builds Jerusalem; He gathers in the exiles of Israel'
With both themes together
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman cites Psalms 147:2 to show that building Jerusalem and gathering Israel's exiles are one idea, so the ending is always 'Who builds Jerusalem'. Rav Sheshet, by contrast, matches the ending to the opening.

quiz.q: Why, according to Shmuel as explained by Rav Naḥman, must one repeat the Amida but not Grace after Meals when Rosh Ḥodesh was forgotten?
o: Rosh Ḥodesh is only mentioned in the Amida, never in Grace
The Amida is an obligation, while Grace depends on eating, which is optional
Grace after Meals is only rabbinic
The Amida is shorter and easier to repeat
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman did not hear the reason from Shmuel but reasoned it out: prayer is obligatory, so one repeats; Grace depends on eating, which one may choose to skip. On Shabbat and Festivals, when eating is required, one does return to the beginning.

quiz.q: How does Abaye resolve the apparent reversal of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda between zimmun (olive vs egg) and returning consecrated meat (egg vs olive)?
o: He reverses the opinions in the mishna about zimmun
He says the two mishnayot were taught by different tanna'im
For zimmun they interpret verses ('eat' vs 'eat and be satisfied'); for consecrated meat they reason by analogy to impurity or to the prohibition
He says Rabbi Meir retracted in one of the cases
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan would reverse one source. Abaye keeps both: in zimmun, Rabbi Meir reads 'eat' as an olive-bulk and 'be satisfied' as drinking, while Rabbi Yehuda reads 'eat and be satisfied' as an egg-bulk; for consecrated meat, Rabbi Meir compares return to impurity (egg-bulk) and Rabbi Yehuda to the prohibition (olive-bulk).
